sections.title: The Lobes of the Brain & Split-Brain Research

blocks.x: Every psychological experience — every idea, mood, and urge — is simultaneously biological. The body is composed of cells that communicate with each other; the brain processes this information, and from it we construct our experience of sights, sounds, meanings, memories, pain, and passion.
The nervous system controls emotions, movement, thinking, and behaviour. It is structurally divided into two parts:

blocks.name: <term d="The brain and spinal cord — where information is processed and decisions are made.">Central Nervous System</term> (CNS)
blocks.def: The brain and spinal cord. The spinal cord transmits most messages between the body and brain.

blocks.name: <term d="All the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, linking them to the rest of the body.">Peripheral Nervous System</term> (PNS)
blocks.def: Smaller nerve branches from the spinal cord that reach the rest of the body, conducting information to and from the CNS.

blocks.x: The PNS divides further into the Somatic Nervous System (SNS) — controls voluntary activities (e.g. lifting a hand) — and the Autonomic Nervous System (ANS) — controls involuntary activities (heartbeat, blood pressure, pupil size).

items: Sympathetic nervous system — prepares the body for emergencies/strenuous activity: speeds the heart, redirects blood to muscles, increases blood pressure, suspends digestion.
Parasympathetic nervous system — conserves energy and aids recovery: reduces heart rate and blood pressure, returns the body to its resting state.

blocks.x: The brain is protected by the skull and sheathing layers; the spinal cord by vertebrae; peripheral nerves by sheathing layers. Spinal cord injury can prevent brain-muscle <term d="The exchange of information between people.">communication</term>, potentially causing paralysis.

Neurons are the elementary components of the nervous system — the human body contains billions of them. Messages travel along nerves (strings of neurons); a <term d="A nerve cell — the basic unit that generates and passes on signals in the nervous system.">neuron</term> can fire hundreds of times a minute.

blocks.name: All-or-none principle
blocks.def: When a neuron fires, it does so at full strength. If not stimulated past the minimum (threshold) level, it does not fire at all.

blocks.x: Three basic parts of a neuron: the cell body (contains nucleus, produces energy), the dendrites (short fibers that receive impulses and send them to the cell body), and the axon (long fiber carrying impulses away from the cell body toward the next neuron's dendrites).

The axon is protected/insulated by the myelin sheath — a white fatty substance that also speeds transmission. In multiple sclerosis, the myelin sheath is destroyed, causing erratic, uncoordinated behaviour. Axon terminals branch out at the axon's end, positioned opposite the next neuron's dendrites.

blocks.name: <term d="The junction where one nerve cell passes its signal on to the next cell.">Synapse</term>
blocks.def: The gap between the axon terminals of one neuron and the dendrites of another. A neuron transmits its message across the synapse by releasing chemicals called neurotransmitters, which can excite the next neuron or inhibit it.

items: Norepinephrine — memory, learning; controls alertness and arousal.
Endorphin — inhibits pain; influences perception of pain/pleasure.
Acetylcholine — movement, memory; enables muscle action.
Dopamine — learning, attention, emotional arousal, movement.
Serotonin — mood, hunger, sleep, arousal.
GABA — major inhibitory neurotransmitter.
Glutamate — major excitatory neurotransmitter; involved in memory.

blocks.x: Clinical links: undersupply of acetylcholine → paralysis, Alzheimer's disease. Oversupply of dopamine → schizophrenia; undersupply → Parkinson's disease (tremors, decreased mobility). Undersupply of norepinephrine/serotonin → depression. Undersupply of GABA → seizures, tremors, insomnia. Oversupply of glutamate → migraines, seizures.
Drugs may act as antagonists (block/inhibit a neurotransmitter's release or effect) or agonists (excite/increase its effect).

items: Afferent (sensory) neurons — relay messages from sense organs to the brain/spinal cord.
Efferent (motor) neurons — send signals from the brain to glands/muscles.
Interneurons — carry impulses between neurons within the CNS, between sensory input and motor output.

blocks.name: 1. The Hindbrain
blocks.def: Rear base of the skull; basic life processes. Includes: Cerebellum (posture, balance, voluntary movement), Medulla (breathing, heart rate, reflexes), Pons (bridge between spinal cord and brain; sleep chemicals).

blocks.name: 2. The Midbrain
blocks.def: Above the pons; integrates sensory information and relays it upward. The medulla, pons, and midbrain together form most of the brain stem. The Reticular Activating System (RAS) spans these structures, alerting the brain to incoming signals and regulating the sleep/wake cycle.

blocks.name: 3. The Forebrain
blocks.def: Covers the brain's central core. Contains the limbic system (hypothalamus, amygdala, thalamus, hippocampus — regulates emotions/motivations), the cerebral cortex (outer layer), and the cerebrum (inner layer).

items: Hypothalamus — hunger, thirst, sexual behaviour, temperature reactions.
Amygdala — controls violent emotions (rage, fear).
Thalamus — integrates sensory input; relay station for nearly all senses except smell.
Hippocampus — important in memory formation.
Cerebral cortex — enables learning, storing complex/abstract information, projecting thinking into the future; site of conscious thinking (planning, reasoning, language, interpreting sensory input).

sections.title: The Lobes of the Brain & Split-Brain Research

blocks.x: The cerebrum has two hemispheres connected by the corpus callosum, roughly mirror images of each other, with deep grooves marking distinct lobes.

items: Occipital lobe — processes visual signals; damage causes visual problems.
Parietal lobe — processes information from senses across the body.
Temporal lobe — hearing, memory, emotion, speaking.
Frontal lobe — organization, planning, creative thinking.

blocks.x: In split-brain operations (used to reduce severe seizures), the corpus callosum is severed, preventing hemisphere communication — a phenomenon called lateralization. E.g. an object in the left hand (processed by the right hemisphere) cannot be verbally named, since language is typically localized in the left hemisphere. Split-brain patients remain largely unchanged in intelligence, personality, and emotion.

items: EEG (electroencephalograph) — records electrical activity; shows if a person is awake, drowsy, or asleep.
Stimulation — can localize malfunctioning brain areas.
Lesions — removing brain areas can reveal their function (e.g. reduced fear/aggression).
Accidents — tragic injuries can reveal brain-behaviour links (e.g. personality change).
CAT (computerized axial tomography) — pinpoints injuries and brain deterioration.
PET (positron emission tomography) — shows which brain areas activate during tasks.
MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) — studies brain structure and activity.

blocks.x: The endocrine system sends chemical messages called hormones, produced in endocrine glands and released directly into the bloodstream. Hormones affect growth of bodily structures, metabolic processes, sex differentiation, stress responses, and directly influence moods and drives.

items: Thyroid gland — produces thyroxine. Too little → hypothyroidism (laziness, lethargy). Too much → hyperthyroidism (weight/sleep loss, overactivity).

Adrenal glands — secrete epinephrine/norepinephrine (adrenaline/noradrenaline — increase heartbeat, breathing, heighten fear/anxiety) and cortical steroids (help muscles, release stored sugar for emergencies).
Sex glands — testes (sperm, testosterone) and ovaries (eggs, estrogen, progesterone). Varying hormone levels can cause PMS (fatigue, irritability, depression).
Pituitary gland — the 'master gland'; releases hormones influencing growth and triggering other glands' hormone release (e.g. triggering sex glands under the brain's influence).

blocks.x: Key distinction: a chemical acting as a neurotransmitter is released right beside the cell it excites/inhibits; as a hormone, it's released into the blood and diffuses throughout the body. E.g. norepinephrine is a hormone when secreted by the adrenal glands into the blood, but a neurotransmitter when released by sympathetic motor neurons.

blocks.name: Heredity
blocks.def: The genetic transmission of characteristics from parents to offspring, via genes — the basic units of heredity.

blocks.x: The nature-nurture debate: Nature = inherited biological makeup. Nurture = environmental factors (family, culture, education, individual experiences).

Twin studies compare identical twins (same genes + environment when raised together) to fraternal twins — if identical twins are more alike on a trait, genes likely matter for that trait. Note: genetic influence doesn't mean behaviour can't change — altering the environment in which genes operate is possible even if the genetic code itself can't be changed.

items: Understanding markers of biological vulnerability helps identify those at greatest risk for psychopathology.
Appreciating that individual differences in neuro-biological traits affect treatment <term d="The reaction produced by a stimulus.">response</term>.
Supports developing new therapeutic approaches for conditions like addiction and depression.

mnemonics.h: SLC — three cues for abnormal behaviour
lines: Statistical infrequency, personal distress, and maladaptive/impaired functioning — the three go-to criteria for spotting abnormal behaviour.

mnemonics.h: HOMER — <term d="Any consequence that makes the behaviour before it more likely to happen again.">reinforcement</term> vs <term d="Any consequence that makes the behaviour before it less likely to happen again.">punishment</term>
lines: Reinforcement always increases a behaviour; punishment always decreases it — regardless of whether something is added (positive) or removed (negative).

mnemonics.h: ABC of <term d="The view that psychology should study only observable behaviour, not private mental states.">behaviourism</term>
lines: Antecedent, Behaviour, Consequence — the basic chain behaviourists analyse to explain why a behaviour keeps happening.

mnemonics.h: DEPC — the four goals of psychology
lines: Describe, Explain/understand, Predict, Control — the four things every psychological study is ultimately trying to do.

<term d="In Freudian theory, the primitive part of the mind demanding immediate gratification.">id</term> (Pleasure), <term d="In Freudian theory, the part of the mind that balances demands against reality.">ego</term> (reality — 'I'), <term d="In Freudian theory, the internalised moral standards of society.">superego</term> (morality — think '<term d="The moral principles governing how research and practice should be conducted.">Ethics</term>') — the three parts constantly negotiating behaviour.
Variable-ratio reinforcement schedules (like gambling) are the hardest to extinguish — Very Resistant to stopping.
